paragraphs.old: [That summer Prue Ramsay died of an illness connected with childbirth. It was a real tragedy, people said. Nobody, they said, had deserved happiness more.]

paragraphs.old: In spring the garden urns, planted by chance with whatever the wind had blown into them, were as bright as ever. Violets came, and then daffodils. Yet the calm and brightness of the day were just as strange as the chaos and uproar of the night. There the trees stood, and there the flowers stood, gazing in front of them, gazing upward, yet seeing nothing at all; they had no eyes, and that made them terrible.

paragraphs.old: She meant no harm by it. The family wouldn’t come, never again, some said, and maybe the house would be sold at Michaelmas, the autumn quarter day. So Mrs. McNab bent down and picked a bunch of flowers to carry home. While she dusted, she set them on the table. She liked flowers. It seemed a shame to let them go to waste. Say the house was sold (and she stood, hands on hips, before the looking glass)—well, it would need seeing to, that it would. All these years it had stood there with nobody in it. The books and all were gone moldy, what with the war and help being so hard to come by; the place hadn’t been cleaned the way she’d have wanted. It would take more than one pair of hands to set it right now. She was too old for it. Her legs hurt. Every one of those books ought to be laid out on the grass in the sun; plaster had come down in the hall; the drainpipe over the study window had got blocked and let the rain in; the carpet was ruined, clean ruined. But folks should come and see for themselves; they should’ve sent someone down to look. There were clothes in the cupboards, after all; they’d left clothes in every bedroom. What was she meant to do with them? The moth was in them—Mrs. Ramsay’s things. Poor lady! She’d never be wanting _them_ again. Dead, they said she was; years back, in London. Here was the old gray cloak she used to garden in (Mrs. McNab ran her fingers over it). She could see her now, as she came up the drive with the washing, bent over her flowers (a pitiful sight the garden was now, run wild, rabbits scuttling out at you from the beds)—could see her in that gray cloak with one of the children by her side. There were boots and shoes; there was a brush and comb left lying on the dressing table, for all the world as if she meant to be back tomorrow. (Went very sudden at the end, they said.) Once they’d been going to come, but they put it off, what with the war and traveling being so hard these days; and all these years they’d never come; only sent her money; never wrote, never came, and expected to find everything just as they left it, oh dear, dear! Why, the drawers in the dressing table were stuffed full (she pulled them open)—handkerchiefs, scraps of ribbon. Yes, she could see Mrs. Ramsay, as she came up the drive with the washing.

paragraphs.old: She heaped up a little mountain for the ants to climb over. Meddling like this in their cosmos, she drove them into a frenzy of indecision. Some scurried one way, some another.
paragraphs.new: She heaped up a little mountain for the ants to climb over. Meddling like this in the making of their world, she drove them into a frenzy of indecision. Some scurried one way, some another.
